questions.question: Leadership ethics guide decision-making by providing ____
questions.explanation: Ethics gives leaders a set of moral principles and standards for judging what is right or wrong when making decisions. Procedural shortcuts (A), justifying authority (B) and performance incentives (D) are not ethical guides; ethics is about doing what is right, not what is convenient or rewarded.

questions.question: The ethical dimension of leadership emphasises ____
questions.explanation: Ethical leadership is about acting with integrity and taking moral responsibility for how decisions affect people. Power maximisation (A) and absolute authority (C) ignore ethics, and focusing on performance outcomes alone (B) leaves out whether the means used were right.

questions.question: In social contract ethics, injustice occurs when __________________
questions.explanation: Social contract ethics judges rules by whether all members could fairly accept them, so injustice arises when an agreement unfairly favours some people over others. Options B, C and D describe change or weakness in a system, which is not in itself unjust.

questions.question: A leader guided by social contract theory bases authority primarily on __________________
questions.explanation: Social contract theory explains government as arising from an agreement among members of society, so a leader's authority rests on collective agreement and the legitimacy it gives. Options B, C and D ground authority in personal feeling, inheritance or religion rather than agreement.

questions.question: Social contract ethics interprets rights as __________________
questions.explanation: In social contract thinking, rights are protections that members of society agree to recognise for one another as part of their agreement. Option D is wrong because people give up some freedoms under the contract, so rights are not unlimited; A and B miss the idea of mutual agreement.

questions.question: Social contract ethics interprets moral obligation as __________________
questions.explanation: Social contract ethics sees moral obligation as a limit that reasonable people freely accept because they benefit from living under shared rules. Option D sounds close, but the point of the contract is that the duty is accepted by agreement, not simply forced on people; B and C miss the role of reason.

questions.question: In social contract reasoning, laws are justified when they __________________

options.b: Align with principles citizens would accept

questions.explanation: Social contract reasoning holds that a law is justified when it rests on principles that free, reasonable citizens would agree to. Option A ignores fairness, while C and D tie laws to the ruler or to existing power rather than to consent.

questions.question: The ethical goal of social contract reasoning is to make social rules __________________
questions.explanation: The aim of social contract reasoning is to arrive at social rules that are fair and that every member of society could reasonably accept. Options A, C and D base rules on dominance, history or emotion rather than fair agreement.

questions.question: Social contract ethics assumes that moral rules gain strength from __________________
questions.explanation: Under social contract ethics, moral rules are strong because members of society share in endorsing them through their agreement. Options B, C and D ground rules in custom, power or fear rather than shared agreement.

questions.question: The social contract explains moral norms as sustained through __________________
questions.explanation: Social contract theory sees moral norms as lasting because people trust that others will keep to the agreement and expect the same of each other. Option A is tempting because fear features in some accounts of life before the contract, but norms in society are sustained by mutual expectation, not fear alone.

questions.question: The social contract theory, as propounded by Rousseau, holds that government legitimacy derives from:

options.d: The consent and agreement of the governed

questions.explanation: Rousseau argued that legitimate authority comes only from an agreement among the people, who together form a sovereign body guided by the general will. Divine right (option C) is the older justification that social contract thinkers rejected, and force or wealth (options A and B) may give power but not legitimacy.

questions.question: Thomas Hobbes' view of the social contract differed from Locke's primarily in that Hobbes believed:

options.a: A powerful sovereign was necessary to prevent the brutish state of nature
options.b: People should retain natural rights even after forming a government
options.c: Property rights are the foundation of all political obligations
options.d: The general will always reflects individual interests

questions.explanation: Hobbes saw life without government as a war of all against all, so he argued that people should surrender their freedom to a strong, absolute sovereign in exchange for peace and security. Option B is Locke's position, option C also reflects Locke's emphasis on property, and option D uses Rousseau's idea of the general will.

questions.question: Corporate governance ethics in the private sector primarily ensures that:

options.a: Organisations act with integrity, transparency and accountability to all stakeholders
options.b: Companies maximise profits irrespective of ethical constraints
options.c: Government directives replace internal corporate codes of conduct
options.d: Only legal compliance is required without voluntary ethical standards

questions.explanation: Ethical corporate governance means a company is directed and controlled in a way that is honest, open and accountable to shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, regulators and the community. Option B ignores ethics altogether, option D treats ethics as mere legal compliance, and option C wrongly suggests companies need no internal codes of their own.

questions.question: Ethical considerations in the public sector differ from those in the private sector primarily because:

options.a: Public sector actors are stewards of public resources and owe accountability to all citizens
options.b: Profit motive is the primary ethical consideration in the public sector
options.c: Private sector ethics are more stringent than public sector requirements
options.d: Public officials are not bound by any code of conduct

questions.explanation: Public officials hold power and funds in trust for the whole population, so their central ethical duties are to avoid abusing office for personal gain and to act in the public interest. Option D is false because public officers have codes of conduct, option B describes the private sector, and option C has no general basis.

questions.question: Which of the following BEST represents a breach of the social contract by a government?

options.b: Holding regular free and fair elections
options.c: Systematically denying citizens access to basic rights and public services

questions.explanation: Under the social contract, citizens accept the authority of government in return for protection of their rights and provision of basic services, so a government that systematically denies these fails its side of the bargain. Taxation laws (option A) are part of the normal contract, and free elections and an independent judiciary (options B and D) are signs that the contract is being kept.

questions.question: The concept of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) reflects which view of business responsibility?

options.a: Pure profit maximisation without external obligations
options.b: Strict compliance with government tax codes only
options.c: A stakeholder-oriented approach where business has responsibilities beyond profit
options.d: Avoidance of all business activities that carry risk

questions.explanation: CSR holds that a business owes duties not only to its owners but also to employees, customers, communities and the environment, so it should act responsibly beyond simply making profit. Option A is the narrow shareholder view that CSR challenges, option B reduces responsibility to tax compliance, and option D has nothing to do with CSR.

questions.question: Which social contract theorist argued that people keep natural rights to life, liberty and property, and may resist a government that violates them?
questions.explanation: John Locke held that government is created by consent to protect natural rights, so a government that violates life, liberty and property breaks the contract and may be resisted or replaced. Hobbes (option D) favoured an absolute sovereign that subjects should not resist, Rousseau (option C) built his theory on the general will, and Machiavelli (option B) was not a social contract theorist.

questions.question: Thomas Hobbes described human life in the state of nature, without government, as:

options.a: Ordered by the divine right of kings
options.b: Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short
options.c: Peaceful but lacking an impartial judge to settle disputes
options.d: Free and equal, until corrupted by society and private property

questions.explanation: Hobbes believed that without a common power to keep order, people would live in a war of all against all, making life solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short, which is why he argued for a strong sovereign. Option C is closer to Locke's milder view of the state of nature, option D reflects Rousseau, and option A is the older theory social contract thinkers rejected.

questions.question: In Rousseau's version of the social contract, legitimate laws must reflect the:
questions.explanation: Rousseau argued that people unite into a sovereign community and that laws are legitimate only when they express the general will, meaning the common good of all citizens. The will of the strongest (option B) is force, not legitimacy, divine will (option D) is the divine right theory, and the interests of property owners (option A) would favour one class over the community.

questions.question: A social contract is best described as:

options.a: An agreement in which people give up certain freedoms and accept a central authority in order to protect their other rights
options.b: A constitution imposed on citizens by a military government
options.c: A trade agreement between two or more countries
options.d: A written employment contract between a government and its civil servants

questions.explanation: The social contract is an implicit agreement among members of a society to cooperate, accepting laws and authority in return for protection and social benefits; it explains why governments have the right to rule. Options D and C are ordinary legal contracts, and an imposed military constitution (option B) lacks the consent that the social contract depends on.

questions.question: Which of the following ethical issues is specific to the public sector rather than the private sector?

options.a: Price-fixing that harms consumers and stifles competition
options.b: Using public office for private gain, such as diverting public funds
options.c: Misleading shareholders through fraudulent company accounts
options.d: Exploiting workers in a company's supply chain

questions.explanation: Public sector ethics centre on abuse of entrusted public authority, such as embezzling public funds, taking kickbacks on government contracts and failing to act in the public interest. Price-fixing (option A), labour exploitation in supply chains (option D) and misleading shareholders (option C) are typical private sector ethical issues arising from profit pressure.

questions.question: When a group of people agree to give up certain rights and accept a central authority in order to protect their other rights, this arrangement is called:
questions.explanation: A social contract is an agreement in which people give up certain rights and accept a central authority so that their other rights are protected. Option D is an ethical problem where personal interests clash with duty, and option A is the system by which a company is directed and controlled. Option C is a hands-off leadership style.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between government and the social contract?

options.a: The social contract is a written document signed by every citizen
options.b: Government and the social contract mean exactly the same thing
options.c: The social contract is what allows any government to work, but the two are different things
options.d: A government can only exist where there is no social contract

questions.explanation: The social contract is the underlying agreement that allows any government to work, but it is not the same thing as the government itself. Option B ignores that distinction. Option A is wrong because the contract is implicit, not a signed document, and option D reverses the relationship.

questions.question: The social contract is best described as which kind of agreement among members of a society?

options.a: A trade agreement between two countries
options.b: An implicit agreement to cooperate for social benefits
options.c: An employment contract between workers and the state
options.d: A written contract enforced by the courts

questions.explanation: The social contract is an implicit, unwritten agreement among members of society to cooperate for social benefits, such as giving up some individual freedom in exchange for state protection. Option D describes a formal legal contract. Options A and C describe specific agreements that are not the social contract.

questions.question: Which of the following is the typical trade-off at the heart of the social contract?

options.a: Surrendering property in exchange for voting rights
options.b: Giving up all rights in exchange for wealth
options.c: Paying bribes in exchange for public services
options.d: Sacrificing some individual freedom in exchange for state protection

questions.explanation: The classic social contract trade-off is giving up some individual freedom in return for protection by the state. Option B exaggerates the bargain. Option C describes corruption, and option A is not the exchange the social contract describes.

questions.question: Theories of the social contract became popular during which period?
questions.explanation: Social contract theories became popular in the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries through thinkers such as Thomas Hobbes, John Locke and Jean-Jacques Rousseau. Options B, D and A give the wrong period.

questions.question: Social contract theories were developed mainly as a means of explaining:

options.a: Why followers should never question leaders
options.b: The origin of government and the obligations of subjects
options.c: How leaders should choose a leadership style

questions.explanation: Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau used the social contract to explain where government comes from and what obligations subjects have toward it. Option D is an accounting question, and option C is a leadership-style question. Option A is not what the theories argue.

questions.question: According to social contract theory, people live together in society in accordance with:

options.a: Market forces of demand and supply alone
options.b: The commands of whoever is strongest at any moment
options.c: An agreement that establishes moral and political rules of behaviour
options.d: Religious rules handed down by a single church

questions.explanation: Social contract theory holds that people live together in line with an agreement that sets moral and political rules of behaviour. Option B describes rule by force, the kind of insecure condition the contract is meant to escape. Options A and D name other forces that are not the basis of the theory.

questions.question: Which of the following thinkers is NOT one of the classical social contract theorists?
questions.explanation: Thomas Hobbes, John Locke and Jean-Jacques Rousseau are the classical social contract theorists of the 17th and 18th centuries. Karl Marx was a 19th-century thinker known for his critique of capitalism, not for social contract theory. Options B, D and A are all social contract theorists.

questions.question: Which social contract theorist described life in the state of nature, without government, as 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short'?
questions.explanation: Thomas Hobbes described the state of nature as a war of all against all in which life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short', which is why he thought people needed a strong sovereign. Option B saw the state of nature as governed by natural law and reason, and option A saw natural man as relatively free and peaceful. Option C is a followership scholar.

questions.question: Thomas Hobbes set out his social contract theory in which work?
questions.explanation: Hobbes presented his social contract theory in Leviathan (1651). Option B is by John Locke, and option D is by Jean-Jacques Rousseau. Option A is Robert Kelley's book on followership.

questions.question: In Hobbes' version of the social contract, people surrender their rights mainly to:

options.b: A general will that is expressed by the whole community
options.c: A limited government that must protect property or be replaced
options.d: A strong, absolute sovereign that guarantees peace and security

questions.explanation: Hobbes believed that, to escape the violent state of nature, people hand their rights to a powerful, absolute sovereign that keeps order and security. Option B reflects Rousseau's idea of the general will, and option C reflects Locke's limited government. Option A is a modern governance idea, not Hobbes' sovereign.

questions.question: John Locke held that people possess natural rights which government exists to protect. These rights are:
questions.explanation: Locke argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that the purpose of government is to protect them. Option D lists social advantages, and option A lists basic needs. Option B lists civic duties and processes, not Locke's natural rights.

questions.question: According to John Locke, if a government violates the natural rights it was created to protect, the people:

options.a: Have the right to resist and replace that government
options.b: Should return to the state of nature permanently
options.c: Must transfer their rights to a foreign power
options.d: Must obey it absolutely to avoid returning to chaos

questions.explanation: Locke's government is limited and rests on the consent of the governed, so if it breaks its trust by violating natural rights, the people may resist and replace it. Option D is closer to Hobbes' view of an absolute sovereign. Options B and C are not part of Locke's argument.

questions.question: Which social contract theorist is associated with the idea of the 'general will' as the basis of legitimate authority?
questions.explanation: Rousseau argued that legitimate authority comes from the general will of the people as a whole, so sovereignty belongs to the people. Option D favoured an absolute sovereign, and option C stressed natural rights and limited government. Option B is a leadership scholar.

questions.question: The famous opening line 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains' comes from which thinker?
questions.explanation: This line opens Rousseau's The Social Contract (1762), where he asks how political authority can be legitimate. Option C is known for the 'nasty, brutish and short' description of the state of nature. Option B is known for natural rights to life, liberty and property, and option D is a leadership scholar.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts Hobbes and Rousseau?

options.a: Hobbes placed sovereignty in the people; Rousseau favoured an absolute monarch
options.b: Both argued that property is the only natural right
options.c: Both argued that people should have no government at all
options.d: Hobbes favoured an absolute sovereign; Rousseau placed sovereignty in the general will of the people

questions.explanation: Hobbes thought only an absolute sovereign could prevent the chaos of the state of nature, while Rousseau located sovereignty in the people through the general will. Option A swaps their positions. Option C is wrong because both justified government, and option B misstates both thinkers, since property was one of Locke's three natural rights.

questions.question: How did John Locke's view of the state of nature differ from that of Thomas Hobbes?

options.a: Both saw it as the ideal condition to return to
options.b: Both saw it as perfectly safe and orderly
options.c: Locke saw it as a war of all against all; Hobbes saw it as peaceful
options.d: Locke saw it as governed by natural law and reason, though insecure; Hobbes saw it as a war of all against all

questions.explanation: For Locke, the state of nature was governed by natural law and reason, but people formed governments to protect their rights more securely. For Hobbes it was a violent war of all against all. Option C reverses the two. Options B and A misstate both, since neither saw the state of nature as something to keep.

questions.question: During violent unrest, a state government imposes a dusk-to-dawn curfew, and residents accept a temporary limit on their movement so that lives and property are protected. This best illustrates:

options.b: A conflict of interest on the part of the governor
options.c: Laissez-faire leadership by the state government
options.d: The social contract, in which citizens give up some freedom for state protection

questions.explanation: Accepting a temporary limit on freedom in return for protection is the social contract at work, and emergency measures that override freedoms are listed among its examples. Option C would mean the government stepping back, not acting. Option B requires a personal interest clashing with public duty, and option A is a transactional leadership practice.

questions.question: Which of the following examples of the social contract is a civic DUTY rather than a right?
questions.explanation: Jury duty is an obligation citizens owe under the social contract, along with paying taxes, census participation and other civic duties. Options B, D and C are rights that the social contract protects for citizens.

questions.question: Every year, a Lagos trader pays N250,000 in taxes, and in return expects the state to provide security, roads and courts. This exchange is best explained by:

options.d: The agency relationship in a company

questions.explanation: Paying taxes and accepting government authority in return for protection and public services is a classic example of the social contract. Option D describes managers acting on behalf of owners in a business. Options B and A are leadership and followership models.

questions.question: Requirements such as registering births and obtaining government identification are listed under the social contract as:
questions.explanation: Registering births and obtaining government identification are administrative requirements that citizens accept as part of the social contract. Option D concerns rights to work and earn, and option C concerns speech. Option A concerns agreements between states.

questions.question: Corporate social responsibility, consumer protection and environmental protection appear among examples of the social contract. This suggests that the social contract:

options.a: Has nothing to do with economic life
options.c: Replaces the need for laws and regulations
options.d: Also shapes what society expects of businesses, not only of governments

questions.explanation: Including CSR, consumer protection and environmental protection shows that the social contract also covers society's expectations of businesses. Options B and A wrongly narrow the idea. Option C is wrong because laws and regulations are themselves listed as examples of the social contract.

questions.question: Ethical issues in the public sector centre mainly on:

options.a: Price-fixing and anti-competitive behaviour among firms
options.c: Exploitation of labour in global supply chains
options.d: Abuse of authority for personal gain, conflicts of interest, corruption and failure to act in the public interest

questions.explanation: Public sector ethical issues centre on abuse of authority for personal gain, conflicts of interest, corruption and failure to act in the public interest. Options A, B and C are ethical issues mainly associated with the profit-driven private sector.

questions.question: Bribery, nepotism, mismanagement of public funds and weak accountability in the public sector mainly:
questions.explanation: These common public sector ethical failures erode public trust in government. Options C, B and A are outcomes of ethical, accountable administration, which these failures undermine.

questions.question: A local government works officer tells a contractor that a N20 million drainage contract will only be approved if the contractor pays him 10 percent in cash. Which public sector ethical issue is this?
questions.explanation: Demanding a kickback to approve a contract is using public office for private gain, which is corruption and bribery. Option D concerns mishandling confidential information, and option B concerns absenteeism and laziness. Option C involves a genuine clash of values, not plain extortion.

questions.question: A state commissioner for lands approves a large land allocation to a company in which he secretly holds shares. Which ethical issue does this primarily illustrate?
questions.explanation: A conflict of interest arises when public officials make decisions that benefit themselves, their family or associates rather than the public, as when the commissioner favours a company he owns shares in. Option D involves confidential information, and option A involves absenteeism and laziness. Option C involves intimidating or harassing people.

questions.question: A director in a federal parastatal promotes his niece to a senior post over three better-qualified officers, purely because she is family. Which public sector ethical issue is this?
questions.explanation: Nepotism and favouritism means hiring, promoting or awarding contracts to friends or family because of the relationship rather than merit. Option B concerns confidential information, and option A concerns absenteeism and laziness. Option D is a private-sector market issue such as price-fixing.

questions.question: A senior officer repeatedly intimidates and threatens a junior colleague who refused to falsify a report. Which public sector ethical issue is this?
questions.explanation: Misuse of power or authority covers intimidating, harassing or discriminating against others by using one's position. Option A involves favouring relatives or friends. Option B involves confidential information, and option D involves absenteeism and laziness.

questions.question: Staff at a government registry access citizens' personal records without authorisation and share some of them on social media. Which public sector ethical issue is this?
questions.explanation: Improper handling of, or unauthorised access to, confidential citizen or government information is a data privacy violation. Option C involves favouring relatives or friends. Option D involves absenteeism and laziness, and option B involves decisions that benefit the official personally.

questions.question: Officers at a ministry routinely sign the attendance register at 8 a.m. and then leave to run private businesses, returning only to sign out. Which public sector ethical issue is this?
questions.explanation: Low integrity and work ethic covers absenteeism, laziness and a lack of dedication to public service, which is what these officers show. Option B involves confidential information, and option C involves official decisions that benefit the decision-maker. Option D involves favouring relatives or friends.

questions.question: A public official must choose between her personal values, pressure from politicians and her professional responsibilities, and the conflict leads to poor administrative judgement. This is described as:
questions.explanation: An ethical dilemma in decision-making is having to choose between personal values, political pressure and professional responsibilities, which often leads to poor administrative judgement. Option A is favouring relatives or friends, and option C is mishandling confidential information. Option B is absenteeism and laziness.

questions.question: Concealing information, making fraudulent reports or avoiding scrutiny in a public agency is classified as:
questions.explanation: Concealing information, filing fraudulent reports and avoiding scrutiny are forms of lack of accountability and transparency, which hinders public trust. Option D is a genuine clash of values, and option B is favouring relatives or friends. Option A is intimidating or harassing people.

questions.question: Addressing ethical challenges in the public sector requires all of the following EXCEPT:

options.b: Restricting citizens' access to public information

questions.explanation: Public sector ethical problems are tackled with strong anti-corruption laws, whistleblower protection, improved transparency and merit-based administration. Restricting access to information reduces transparency and makes things worse. Options A, D and C are all recommended remedies.

questions.question: A ministry wants to stop the practice of awarding posts to relatives of senior officials. Which remedy most directly addresses this problem?
questions.explanation: Nepotism means appointing people because of relationships rather than merit, so a focus on merit-based administration attacks it directly. Option D addresses data privacy, and option C addresses anti-competitive private-sector behaviour. Option A does not deal with how posts are filled.

questions.question: Whistleblower protection helps address public sector ethical problems mainly by:

options.a: Encouraging insiders to report wrongdoing without fear of reprisal
options.b: Guaranteeing jobs for relatives of senior staff
options.c: Keeping corruption cases out of the media
options.d: Allowing officials to avoid public scrutiny

questions.explanation: Protecting whistleblowers makes it safer for insiders to expose corruption and misconduct, which strengthens accountability. Options D and C reduce transparency, and option B describes nepotism.

questions.question: Ethical issues in the private sector primarily arise from:

options.b: The obligation to serve the general public welfare

questions.explanation: Private sector ethical problems mostly come from profit-driven decision-making, which can lead to conflicts of interest, discrimination, harassment and environmental harm. Options A and D are more typical of public sector settings. Option B is the main objective of public enterprises, not the cause of private sector problems.

questions.question: Three cement manufacturers secretly agree to sell a bag at not less than N9,500 so that none of them undercuts the others. Which private sector ethical issue is this?
questions.explanation: Price-fixing is an anti-competitive practice that harms consumers and stifles fair competition. Option D concerns mistreating employees, and option A concerns mishandling customer information. Option C concerns environmental harm and unfair labour practices.

questions.question: To meet investors' expectations, the finance team of a listed company records N800 million of sales that never took place. Which private sector ethical issue is this?
questions.explanation: Recording fictitious sales is dishonest financial reporting, which falls under financial integrity and fraud. Option B concerns practices such as price-fixing. Option D concerns mistreating staff, and option C concerns protecting customer information.

questions.question: A food processing company dumps untreated waste into a river used by nearby villages and buys raw materials from suppliers known to use child labour. Which private sector ethical issue is this?
questions.explanation: Neglecting environmental impacts and failing to ensure safe, fair labour practices across the supply chain are environmental and social responsibility failures. Option C concerns practices such as price-fixing. Option B concerns dishonest reporting, and option D concerns customer information.

questions.question: A private company repeatedly passes over a well-qualified employee for promotion because of her religion. Which private sector ethical issue is this?
questions.explanation: Mistreating employees because of race, gender or religion is workplace harassment and discrimination, which creates toxic environments and violates employee rights. Option C concerns market practices like price-fixing. Option B concerns dishonest reporting, and option D concerns environmental harm and supply-chain labour.

questions.question: A fintech app stores customers' card details and BVNs with weak protection, and hackers steal the records of thousands of users. Which private sector ethical issue does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Misusing, or failing to adequately protect, consumers' personal and financial information is a data privacy and security issue that breaches customer trust. Option A concerns practices such as price-fixing. Option C concerns mistreating staff, and option D concerns personal interests compromising professional judgement.

questions.question: Ethical issues in the private sector are said to often stem from:

options.b: Intense pressure for performance, leading to unethical shortcuts

questions.explanation: Private sector ethical problems often come from intense pressure to perform, which tempts people into unethical shortcuts that risk legal consequences and reputational damage. Options C, D and A are not given as the root of these problems.

questions.question: Which of the following ethical issues appears among BOTH the public sector issues and the private sector issues?

options.a: Neglect of environmental impacts in the supply chain
options.c: Absenteeism and low dedication to public service

questions.explanation: Conflicts of interest appear in both lists: in the public sector as officials benefiting themselves or associates, and in the private sector as personal interests such as nepotism compromising professional judgement. Options B and A are listed only for the private sector, and option C only for the public sector.

questions.question: John Locke presented his theory of government by consent and natural rights in which work?
questions.explanation: Locke set out his ideas on natural rights and government by consent in Two Treatises of Government. Option C is Thomas Hobbes' work, and option A is Jean-Jacques Rousseau's. Option D is James MacGregor Burns' 1978 book on transforming and transactional leadership.

questions.question: Corruption and bribery in the public sector include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Corruption and bribery means using public office for private gain, including accepting kickbacks, stealing public funds and manipulating contracts. Taking approved annual leave is a normal entitlement, not an ethical breach. Options C, B and D are all listed forms of corruption.

questions.question: Crisis communication becomes a governance priority primarily because ____

options.a: Legal departments mandate frequent public statements
options.b: Internal reporting structures demand daily updates
options.c: Media organizations require constant content during emergencies
options.d: Unmanaged information gaps intensify public uncertainty and distrust

questions.explanation: In a crisis, if official information is missing or unclear, rumours fill the gap and public uncertainty and distrust grow, so managing communication becomes a governance priority. Legal requirements (A), internal reporting demands (B) and media appetite for content (C) may exist, but they are not the main reason crisis communication matters for governance.

questions.question: Stakeholder engagement enhances governance adaptability by incorporating __________________
questions.explanation: Bringing different stakeholders into governance adds diverse perspectives, which helps institutions spot new problems and adjust their policies. Options B, C and D describe sameness, fixed rules and top-down orders, which make governance less adaptable, not more.

questions.question: Public governance strengthens service delivery by __________________
questions.explanation: Public governance improves service delivery by making sure processes and resources are aligned with the objectives the service is meant to achieve. Options A, B and D weaken oversight and evaluation, which usually makes service delivery worse.

questions.question: Public governance emphasizes long-term societal outcomes because __________________
questions.explanation: Public policies on matters such as education, health and the environment affect not just today's citizens but future generations, so public governance must look at long-term outcomes. Option A is wrong because efficiency still matters, and options B and C are not reasons governments focus on the long term.

questions.question: Stakeholder engagement supports innovation in governance by encouraging __________________
questions.explanation: Engaging stakeholders brings different groups together to work on problems jointly, and this collaborative problem-solving produces new ideas. Options A, B and D describe closed or rigid processes that discourage innovation.

questions.question: Stakeholder engagement supports governance adaptability by facilitating __________________ feedback.
questions.explanation: Governance can only adjust to change if it keeps hearing from stakeholders, so engagement supports adaptability through continuous feedback. Options A, B and D limit or slow the feedback, making it harder for institutions to respond.

questions.question: Stakeholder participation enhances service delivery when it __________________
questions.explanation: Stakeholder participation improves service delivery when the views of service users are fed into how the service is designed. Option B keeps the focus on internal rules instead of users, and A and C shut users out or make the service rigid.

questions.question: Stakeholder engagement in public governance is closely linked to the principle of __________________
questions.explanation: Engaging stakeholders means sharing information with them and explaining decisions, so it goes hand in hand with transparency. Option D is the opposite, and B and C keep institutions closed to outside input.

questions.question: A benefit of stakeholder participation is enhanced __________________, supporting trust-based governance relationships.
questions.explanation: When people participate in governance, decisions and information are shared more openly, which strengthens transparency norms and builds trust. Options B, C and D are signs of closed governance that participation helps to remove.

questions.question: Stakeholder-based governance enhances accountability by:
questions.explanation: When many stakeholders have a recognised role in governance, each group can watch, question and check the others, so no actor escapes scrutiny. This mutual monitoring is what makes those in authority answerable. Option D is tempting because responsibility is shared, but diffused responsibility makes it harder to hold anyone to account, while options B and C weaken accountability outright.

questions.question: Open consultation forums in governance primarily strengthen:
questions.explanation: Open consultation forums, such as public hearings and town hall meetings, give citizens and stakeholders a direct voice in decisions before they are made, which is the essence of participation. Option A, supervision, is about overseeing work rather than involving people, and rigidity and hierarchy (options C and D) are the opposite of what open forums aim for.

questions.question: Stakeholder engagement strengthens democracy by:
questions.explanation: Stakeholder engagement opens more ways for citizens and groups to take part in decisions, such as consultations, hearings and partnerships, which deepens democracy beyond voting at elections. Options A, C and D all shrink the space for public input, so they weaken democracy rather than strengthen it.

questions.question: A stakeholder in public governance is BEST defined as:

options.a: International organisations that fund national development
options.b: Elected politicians and appointed public officials only
options.c: Only shareholders of listed public companies
options.d: Any individual, group or organisation that can affect or is affected by government decisions and policies

questions.explanation: A stakeholder is anyone who can influence, or is influenced by, a decision, which in public governance includes citizens, communities, businesses, civil society, public servants and development partners. Options C, B and A each pick out only one group and leave out most of the people affected by public policy.

questions.question: Effective stakeholder engagement in governance requires:

options.a: Limiting public participation to technical experts
options.b: Inclusive, transparent and meaningful participation of all relevant parties in decision-making
options.c: Informing stakeholders only after major decisions have been made
options.d: Prioritising media engagement over community involvement

questions.explanation: Good engagement brings affected groups into the process early, shares information openly and gives their views real weight in the final decision. Option C is tempting because informing people is part of engagement, but telling them only after decisions are made is announcement, not engagement, and options A and D exclude many of those affected.

questions.question: Crisis communication management in the public sector is critical because:

options.a: Silence during a crisis protects government from legal liability
options.b: Only international media coverage determines crisis management success
options.c: Crisis management is exclusively a function of the military command
options.d: Timely, accurate and empathetic communication maintains public trust and enables effective crisis response

questions.explanation: During a crisis people need quick, correct and caring information to stay safe and cooperate with authorities, and good communication protects the credibility of government. Silence (option A) usually breeds rumours and distrust, while options B and C wrongly narrow crisis management to the media or the military.

questions.question: Which of the following is the FIRST stage in a typical crisis management cycle?
questions.explanation: Crisis management begins before anything goes wrong, with identifying risks, preventing what can be prevented and preparing plans, teams and supplies. Response (option C) follows once a crisis occurs, recovery and evaluation (option A) come last, and communication (option D) runs through every stage rather than being the first one.

questions.question: In stakeholder theory, stakeholders are typically prioritised based on their:

options.a: Financial contribution to the organisation or government
options.c: Power, legitimacy and urgency of their claims
options.d: Media visibility and public relations capacity

questions.explanation: Mitchell, Agle and Wood's stakeholder salience model says managers pay most attention to stakeholders who have power to influence the organisation, a legitimate claim and an urgent demand. Financial contribution (option A) and media visibility (option D) may give some power, but they are only parts of one attribute, and location (option B) is not a criterion at all.

questions.question: A government's failure to communicate effectively during a national security crisis is likely to result in:

options.a: A reduction in the spread of misinformation
options.b: Public panic, spread of misinformation and erosion of institutional credibility
options.c: Improved operational security for government agencies
options.d: Enhanced public trust and voluntary cooperation

questions.explanation: When government is silent or unclear in a crisis, rumours fill the gap, people panic and citizens lose confidence in the institutions meant to protect them. Options D and A describe the results of good communication, not poor communication, and option C confuses careful handling of sensitive details with failing to communicate at all.

questions.question: In the Mitchell, Agle and Wood (1997) stakeholder salience model, a stakeholder who possesses power, legitimacy and urgency is classified as a:
questions.explanation: The salience model says that the more of the three attributes a stakeholder has, the more attention it deserves, and a stakeholder with all three is definitive and needs immediate priority. A dormant stakeholder (option D) has only power, a discretionary stakeholder (option A) has only legitimacy, and a dependent stakeholder (option B) has legitimacy and urgency but lacks power.

questions.question: In the stakeholder salience model, 'urgency' refers to:

options.a: The degree to which a stakeholder's claim is time-sensitive and critical, calling for immediate attention
options.b: The number of people a stakeholder group represents
options.c: The extent to which a stakeholder's claim is seen as proper or appropriate
options.d: The ability of a stakeholder to impose its will on the organisation

questions.explanation: Urgency captures how pressing a claim is: whether delay would be unacceptable and whether the matter is important to the stakeholder. Option D describes power and option C describes legitimacy, the model's other two attributes, while group size (option B) is not one of the attributes at all.

questions.question: Stakeholder engagement in public governance is best defined as:

options.a: Publicising government programmes through the media
options.b: The process by which government involves those who affect or are affected by its decisions in shaping and implementing them
options.c: Consulting only senior government officials before making decisions
options.d: Announcing policies to the public after they have been finalised

questions.explanation: Stakeholder engagement means bringing citizens, communities, businesses and civil society into policy processes early and genuinely, so their views influence what is decided and how it is carried out. Announcing finished policies (option D) or publicity (option A) is one-way communication, and consulting only officials (option C) leaves out the people affected.

questions.question: Which of the following is a widely accepted principle of effective crisis communication?

options.a: Let different agencies release different messages
options.b: Say nothing until every fact is fully confirmed
options.c: Communicate early, accurately and consistently, and show empathy
options.d: Deny the crisis to avoid causing panic

questions.explanation: Effective crisis communication means being first with information, being right, being credible by speaking consistently, and showing empathy for those affected. Waiting for every fact (option B) leaves a gap that rumours fill, mixed messages (option A) destroy credibility, and denial (option D) usually backfires once the truth emerges.

questions.question: A likely consequence of poor stakeholder engagement in public policy implementation is:

options.c: Stronger public ownership of the policy
options.d: Resistance, low compliance and conflict over the policy

questions.explanation: When people affected by a policy are not consulted, they often feel excluded, misunderstand the policy or see it as unfair, so they resist it, fail to comply or protest. Public ownership, smooth implementation and trust (options C, A and B) are the benefits of good engagement, not consequences of poor engagement.

questions.question: Any group or individual who can affect, or is affected by, the achievement of an organisation's objectives is called a ____.
questions.explanation: A stakeholder is anyone who can affect or is affected by what an organisation does, which makes the idea much wider than ownership. Option A is narrower: a shareholder is only an owner who has invested capital. Options C and D describe particular roles that some stakeholders play, not the general term.

questions.question: Which statement BEST distinguishes stakeholder theory from the shareholder-primacy view of the firm?

options.a: Stakeholder theory says managers should weigh the interests of all affected groups, not only the owners' returns
options.b: Stakeholder theory says profits should be ignored completely in favour of social goals
options.c: Stakeholder theory says only shareholders and directors have legitimate claims on the firm
options.d: Stakeholder theory says government should own every firm that affects the public

questions.explanation: Stakeholder theory holds that a firm owes attention to employees, customers, suppliers, communities and others, not just to shareholders' returns. Option C actually describes shareholder primacy. Option B goes too far, because the theory balances profit with other interests rather than ignoring it, and Option D confuses the theory with state ownership.

questions.question: A manager who argues that 'the main responsibility of a business is to maximise returns to its owners within the law' is expressing the ____.
questions.explanation: Putting owners' returns first, subject only to the law, is the shareholder-primacy position. Option A is the opposite view, which asks managers to balance many groups' interests. Options B and C come from political philosophy and leadership respectively and say nothing specific about whose returns come first.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about shareholders and stakeholders is correct?

options.a: Every stakeholder is a shareholder, but not every shareholder is a stakeholder
options.b: Shareholders and stakeholders are exactly the same group of people
options.c: Shareholders are never counted among a firm's stakeholders
options.d: Every shareholder is a stakeholder, but not every stakeholder is a shareholder

questions.explanation: Shareholders are one group of stakeholders, alongside employees, customers, suppliers, regulators and the community. Option A reverses the relationship, Option B ignores all the non-owner groups, and Option C wrongly removes owners from the stakeholder list.

questions.question: In the context of corporate governance, the board of directors is BEST described as ____.

options.a: the executives who run the company's day-to-day operations
options.b: the government bodies that enforce laws on corporate governance
options.c: a group elected by shareholders to represent their interests and oversee management
options.d: the workforce that carries out the company's operations

questions.explanation: The board is elected by shareholders to represent them and to oversee management. Option A describes management, Option B describes regulators, and Option D describes employees, each of which is a separate stakeholder group.

questions.question: In corporate governance, the government bodies that enforce laws and regulations related to how companies are governed are referred to as ____.
questions.explanation: Regulators are the public bodies that enforce governance laws and rules on companies. Option A provides goods, services or other resources, Option B runs daily operations, and Option D oversees management on behalf of shareholders.

questions.question: Kwara Cement Ltd buys limestone, bags and diesel from several Nigerian firms under long-term contracts. In stakeholder terms, these firms are the company's ____.
questions.explanation: Firms that provide a company with goods, services or other resources are its suppliers and partners. Option A would be government enforcement bodies, Option B would be buyers of the cement, and Option C would be the owners who invested capital.

questions.question: Primary stakeholders of an organisation are BEST described as those who ____.

options.a: have a direct, formal stake in the organisation and are essential to its survival, such as employees, customers and owners
options.b: only comment on the organisation from outside, such as the media and pressure groups
options.c: have no interest in the organisation but hold great power over it
options.d: are always government agencies that license the organisation

questions.explanation: Primary stakeholders have a direct, ongoing relationship with the organisation, and it could not continue without them; employees, customers, owners and suppliers are typical examples. Option B describes secondary stakeholders, who influence the organisation indirectly. Options C and D are not definitions of primary stakeholders at all.

questions.question: An environmental NGO in Port Harcourt campaigns against an oil company's gas flaring but has no contract or ownership link with the company. The NGO is BEST classified as a ____ stakeholder.
questions.explanation: Secondary stakeholders influence or are affected by an organisation without a direct transactional or ownership link, and campaign groups and the media are classic examples. Option A would require a direct stake such as employment, ownership or a contract, and Option C would mean being inside the organisation. Option D is a salience label for a group that holds power, legitimacy and urgency together, which the stem does not establish.

questions.question: Which of the following is an INTERNAL stakeholder of a commercial bank in Lagos?
questions.explanation: Internal stakeholders are people within the organisation, such as employees and managers. Option B is an external regulator, Option C is a group of external customers, and Option D is an external community group.

questions.question: The process of identifying an organisation's stakeholders and positioning them according to attributes such as power and interest, in order to plan how to engage each group, is known as ____.
questions.explanation: Stakeholder mapping identifies who the stakeholders are and places them on a chart, such as a power/interest grid, so that engagement can be planned. Option A reviews crisis readiness, Option B compares performance against others, and Option C prepares future leaders.

questions.question: When carrying out a stakeholder analysis for a new policy, which task should normally come FIRST?

options.a: Deciding how often to send newsletters to each group
options.b: Identifying all the groups that can affect or be affected by the policy
options.c: Evaluating how satisfied each group was with the engagement
options.d: Choosing a spokesperson for media briefings

questions.explanation: Stakeholders must be identified before they can be analysed, prioritised or engaged. Option A is a later planning task that depends on knowing who the groups are. Option C is an evaluation step at the end, and Option D is a communication detail.

questions.question: The two dimensions used in the classic power/interest grid for stakeholder mapping are ____.
questions.explanation: The power/interest grid plots how much influence a stakeholder has against how much they care about the issue. Options A and C mix in attributes from the separate salience model, which uses power, legitimacy and urgency. Option D is demographic data, not a mapping dimension.

questions.question: On a power/interest grid, stakeholders with HIGH power and HIGH interest should generally be ____.

options.d: managed closely (fully engaged as key players)

questions.explanation: Groups that are both powerful and very interested are key players, so they need close, active engagement. Option A is the usual approach for high-power, low-interest groups, Option B suits low-power, high-interest groups, and Option C suits groups low on both.

questions.question: On a power/interest grid, stakeholders with HIGH power but LOW interest should generally be ____.
questions.explanation: Powerful groups with little interest should be kept satisfied so that they do not become opponents, without overloading them with detail. Option A is for groups with both high power and high interest, and Option C is for interested groups with little power. Option D is wrong because no mapped stakeholder is simply ignored, especially a powerful one.

questions.question: On a power/interest grid, stakeholders with LOW power but HIGH interest should generally be ____.
questions.explanation: Groups that care a lot but have little influence should be kept informed through regular, adequate communication, and they can be useful allies. Option A fits powerful but uninterested groups, Option B fits key players, and Option D fits groups low on both power and interest.

questions.question: On a power/interest grid, stakeholders with LOW power and LOW interest should generally be ____.
questions.explanation: Groups low on both power and interest need only light monitoring in case their position changes. Options B, C and D are the strategies for the other three quadrants and would spend too much effort on this group.

questions.question: Lagos State plans a new bus rapid transit corridor. The traders' association along the route is very worried about the project but has little influence over the final decision. Using a power/interest grid, the BEST approach to this association is to ____.

options.c: manage them closely as key players

questions.explanation: High interest with low power places the traders in the 'keep informed' quadrant, so they should get regular, clear information about the project. Option A is for powerful groups with low interest, and Option C is for groups with both high power and high interest. Option D would ignore how much the traders care about the project.

questions.question: A federal ministry must approve funding for a state road project but pays little attention to its details. On a power/interest grid, the project team should treat the ministry as a group to ____.
questions.explanation: The ministry has high power, since it controls the funds, but low interest, so it falls in the 'keep satisfied' quadrant. Option A is for interested groups with little power. Options C and D risk upsetting a group that could stop the project.

questions.question: A key risk of neglecting a 'keep satisfied' stakeholder (high power, low interest) is that ____.

options.a: the stakeholder will automatically lose all its power
options.b: the stakeholder may become interested and use its power to block the organisation's plans
options.c: the stakeholder will become a low-interest, low-power group
options.d: the stakeholder will become a supplier of the organisation

questions.explanation: Powerful stakeholders can quickly become interested if they feel ignored, and they then move into the key-player quadrant with the ability to block decisions. Option A is wrong because neglect does not reduce a group's power. Options C and D do not follow from neglect at all.

questions.question: In stakeholder salience analysis, the degree to which a stakeholder's claim calls for immediate attention is called ____.
questions.explanation: Urgency describes how time-sensitive or pressing a claim is. Option A is whether the claim is seen as proper or appropriate, and Option B is the ability to impose one's will on the organisation. Option C belongs to the separate power/interest grid, not the salience model.

questions.question: In stakeholder salience analysis, the general perception that a stakeholder's claim or actions are desirable, proper or appropriate is called ____.
questions.explanation: Legitimacy is the attribute of a claim that is socially accepted as proper or appropriate. Option A is about how pressing the claim is, and Option C is about the stakeholder's ability to influence outcomes. Option D is not one of the three salience attributes.

questions.question: In stakeholder salience analysis, a stakeholder that possesses power, legitimacy AND urgency at the same time is called a ____ stakeholder.
questions.explanation: Holding all three attributes makes a stakeholder definitive, and managers must give such a group immediate priority. Option B has power only, Option C has legitimacy and urgency but lacks power, and Option D has urgency only.

questions.question: After a flood, residents of a riverside community in Kogi State have a legitimate and urgent claim for relief, but they have little power to force the state agency to act. In stakeholder salience terms, they are BEST described as ____ stakeholders.
questions.explanation: A dependent stakeholder has legitimacy and urgency but lacks power, so it relies on others to advocate for it. Option A would require power as well, Option C has power only, and Option D combines power and legitimacy without urgency.

questions.question: A large trade union has the power to call a strike against a government agency, but at present it has no claim pending and no urgent issue. In stakeholder salience terms, the union is currently a ____ stakeholder.
questions.explanation: A dormant stakeholder has power but, for now, neither a legitimate claim nor an urgent one, so it could become important quickly if an issue arises. Option A would need all three attributes. Option B has legitimacy and urgency without power, and Option C has only urgency.

questions.question: Which pairing of stakeholder theory perspectives is correct?

options.a: Instrumental: firms have a moral duty to consider stakeholders; Normative: attending to stakeholders improves profit
options.b: Instrumental: describes how firms actually behave; Normative: predicts share prices
options.c: Instrumental: attending to stakeholders helps the firm perform better; Normative: firms have a moral duty to consider stakeholders
options.d: Instrumental: applies only to government; Normative: applies only to private firms

questions.explanation: The instrumental view treats stakeholder management as a means to better performance, while the normative view says stakeholders deserve consideration for moral reasons. Option A swaps the two. Option B confuses the instrumental view with the descriptive one, and Option D invents a public/private split.

questions.question: The use of stakeholder theory simply to explain how organisations actually behave towards their stakeholders, without judging whether that behaviour is right, is called the ____ perspective.
questions.explanation: The descriptive perspective reports what organisations really do in dealing with stakeholders. Option B prescribes what they ought to do on moral grounds, and Option C links stakeholder management to performance. Option D is a leadership style, not a stakeholder perspective.

questions.question: On a spectrum of public participation running from least to most public influence, which level is the LOWEST?
questions.explanation: Informing is one-way communication that gives people balanced information but no say in the decision, so it sits at the bottom of the spectrum. Option B at least collects feedback. Options C and D give the public progressively more influence, and empowering places the final decision in public hands.

questions.question: On a spectrum of public participation, the level at which final decision-making is placed in the hands of the public is called ____.
questions.explanation: Empowering is the highest level of participation because the public itself makes the final decision, as in a binding referendum or citizen budget vote. Option A only shares information, Option C seeks feedback, and Option D works with the public throughout while the authority still decides.

questions.question: A local government council in Ogun State publishes its draft budget and holds town-hall meetings to collect residents' comments before councillors finalise it. This level of participation is BEST described as ____.
questions.explanation: Consulting means obtaining public feedback on proposals while the authority keeps the final decision, which is what the council is doing. Option A would only publish the budget without seeking views. Options B and D would hand the final decision to residents, which the stem does not describe.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a realistic benefit of effective stakeholder engagement in public governance?

options.a: It increases the legitimacy of decisions
options.b: It improves the quality of information used in decisions
options.c: It builds public ownership of policies and reduces conflict
options.d: It guarantees that every stakeholder gets exactly what it wants

questions.explanation: Engagement helps balance interests, but no process can give every group exactly what it wants, because interests often conflict. Options A, B and C are genuine benefits: engaged groups see decisions as more legitimate, add local knowledge, and are more likely to support the policies that result.

questions.question: Before relocating a motor park in Ibadan, the state government holds sessions only with transport union leaders, leaving out traders, commuters and persons with disabilities. Which principle of good stakeholder engagement is MOST clearly breached?
questions.explanation: Inclusive engagement reaches all affected groups, especially vulnerable ones, rather than only the loudest or most organised. Option B is a salience attribute, not an engagement principle. Options C and D would make the process even narrower.

questions.question: Corporate governance, in its simplest sense, refers to ____.

options.a: the rules, practices and processes by which a company is directed and controlled
options.b: the day-to-day selling and marketing activities of a company
options.c: the process of setting the prices of a company's products
options.d: the government's power to tax company profits

questions.explanation: Corporate governance is the system of rules, practices and processes through which a company is directed and controlled, balancing the interests of its many stakeholders. Option B describes operations, not governance. Option C is a pricing decision, and Option D is fiscal policy.

questions.question: An unexpected event that threatens an organisation's operations, reputation or stakeholders, and forces decisions under time pressure and uncertainty, is called a ____.
questions.explanation: A crisis combines threat, surprise, uncertainty and time pressure. Option B is handled by normal procedures without serious threat. Option C is a planned document, and Option D is an ordinary accounting difference.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a typical characteristic of a crisis?

options.c: It is routine and fully predictable
options.d: It leaves little time for decisions

questions.explanation: Crises are marked by serious threat, uncertainty and urgency, which is why ordinary routines are not enough. A routine, fully predictable event is handled by normal procedures, so it is not a crisis. Options A, B and D are all standard features of a crisis.

questions.question: Which of the following activities belongs to the PRE-CRISIS stage of crisis management?

options.a: Preparing a crisis communication plan and training spokespersons
options.b: Issuing a holding statement after an explosion
options.c: Reviewing lessons learned after the crisis has ended
options.d: Rebuilding the organisation's reputation after a scandal

questions.explanation: The pre-crisis stage covers prevention and preparation, such as scanning for warning signs, writing plans and training spokespersons. Option B is a response activity during the crisis. Options C and D belong to the post-crisis stage of recovery and learning.

questions.question: Which of the following activities belongs to the POST-CRISIS stage of crisis management?

options.a: Scanning the environment for early warning signs
options.c: Evaluating how the crisis was handled and updating the crisis plan
options.d: Announcing the first facts of an incident to the media

questions.explanation: After the crisis, the organisation evaluates its response, learns lessons, continues follow-up communication and updates its plan. Options A and B are preparation activities in the pre-crisis stage. Option D happens during the crisis response itself.

questions.question: The collection, processing and sharing of information needed to deal with a crisis situation, with affected stakeholders and the public, is known as ____.
questions.explanation: Crisis communication is the gathering and sharing of information during a crisis, both inside the organisation and with external stakeholders. Option B is paid messaging on policy issues. Option C is a financial planning task, and Option D is about how important stakeholders are.

questions.question: A short statement released very quickly after a crisis breaks, which acknowledges the incident, expresses concern and promises further updates before all facts are known, is called a ____.
questions.explanation: A holding statement lets the organisation speak first and show concern while it gathers the facts. Option A delays publication of information, and Option B is a yearly performance document. Option C stops people from speaking, which is the opposite of early communication.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT generally regarded as good practice in crisis communication?

options.a: Communicating early, even if only to say what is known so far
options.b: Making sure information released is accurate
options.d: Responding to media questions with 'no comment' until the crisis is over

questions.explanation: Saying 'no comment' is usually read as hiding something, and it leaves a gap that rumour and speculation fill. Options A, B and C reflect widely accepted principles: be first, be right, be credible and show empathy.

questions.question: During a cholera outbreak in Bauchi, three state officials give journalists three different death tolls on the same day. Which crisis communication practice would MOST directly have prevented this?

options.a: Releasing no figures at all until the outbreak ends
options.b: Using a single designated spokesperson and coordinated, verified messages
options.c: Allowing every official to brief the press independently
options.d: Communicating only through rumour on social media

questions.explanation: A designated spokesperson working from verified, coordinated figures keeps messages consistent and credible. Option A creates an information vacuum that rumours fill, and Option C is what caused the confusion in the first place. Option D would make the misinformation worse.

questions.question: A Lagos food company discovers that one batch of its yoghurt is contaminated. Which response BEST reflects sound crisis communication?

options.a: Quietly withdraw the batch and say nothing to avoid bad publicity
options.b: Deny any problem until a customer falls sick
options.c: Promptly recall the batch and tell the public honestly what is known, what is being done and how to get refunds
options.d: Blame the retailers who stocked the product

questions.explanation: Fast, honest communication combined with corrective action protects consumers and preserves trust. Options A and B hide a safety risk, which is unethical and usually backfires when the truth comes out. Option D shifts blame instead of solving the problem.

questions.question: During a crisis, a company publicly blames an outside party, such as a supplier, entirely for the problem. This crisis response strategy is called ____.
questions.explanation: Scapegoating is a denial-type strategy that puts the blame on some person or group outside the organisation. Option A accepts responsibility, and Option C fixes the problem and prevents it from happening again. Option D reminds stakeholders of the organisation's past good deeds.

questions.question: When an organisation is clearly at fault for a preventable crisis, which response is MOST likely to protect long-term trust?

options.b: Attacking those who reported the problem
options.c: Staying silent until public attention fades
options.d: Accepting responsibility, apologising and taking corrective action

questions.explanation: When responsibility is clear, rebuilding strategies such as an apology, compensation and corrective action are the most credible way to restore trust. Options A and B are denial strategies that badly damage credibility once the facts are known. Option C leaves an information vacuum.

questions.question: Why should an organisation inform its own employees early during a crisis?

options.a: Employees are legally the only group that must be told
options.b: Employees have no role in how outsiders see the crisis
options.c: Employees act as informal spokespersons, and learning the facts first from the media damages morale and spreads confusion
options.d: Informing employees removes the need to inform the public

questions.explanation: Employees are a key internal stakeholder group. They talk to customers, family and the media, so they need accurate information early. Option A is false, and Option B ignores their influence. Option D is wrong because the public still has to be informed.

questions.question: During a fuel scarcity, false messages claiming that all filling stations in Abuja will shut for a week spread rapidly on WhatsApp. The MOST appropriate action for the responsible agency is to ____.

options.a: ignore social media because only newspapers matter
options.b: wait until the scarcity ends before saying anything
options.c: monitor social media and quickly correct the false claims with verified information through official channels
options.d: shut down all social media in the city

questions.explanation: Social media spreads rumours fast, so monitoring them and quickly correcting falsehoods with verified facts is central to modern crisis communication. Options A and B let the rumour grow. Option D is a heavy-handed restriction that harms public trust.

questions.question: Which of the following would NOT normally be part of a crisis management plan?

options.a: A list of crisis team members and their roles
options.b: Up-to-date contact details for key stakeholders and media
options.c: A promise that the organisation will never face a crisis

questions.explanation: A crisis plan prepares for crises that may happen; it cannot promise that none will occur. Options A, B and D are standard contents of a crisis plan: who does what, whom to contact, and ready-made messages and procedures.

questions.question: A government agency sets up a toll-free hotline during a disease outbreak so that citizens can ask questions and report cases. This mainly reflects the crisis communication principle of ____.
questions.explanation: A hotline lets the agency both give information and receive it from the public, which improves its response and builds trust. Option A describes communication that never listens. Options B and D work against openness.

questions.question: Which group would MOST appropriately be included on a public organisation's crisis management team?

options.a: Only junior staff from the public relations unit
options.d: Senior decision-makers, a communications lead, legal advice and the heads of the affected operations

questions.explanation: A crisis team needs people with authority, communication skills, legal knowledge and operational expertise so it can decide and act quickly. Option A lacks authority, and Options B and C are external stakeholders the team communicates with, not the people who manage the crisis.

questions.question: The process by which public institutions manage resources, implement policies and deliver services to citizens is called:
questions.explanation: Public governance is the process by which public institutions manage resources, implement policies and deliver services to citizens. Option A concerns how business organisations are directed and controlled, Option D is one step in engaging stakeholders, and Option C deals with sudden threatening events.

questions.question: Effective public governance depends mainly on:

options.b: The number of ministries a government creates
options.d: The personal wealth of political leaders

questions.explanation: Effective public governance depends on stakeholder participation, because those who are affected by policies help shape, accept and monitor them. Option A undermines transparency, while Options D and B have no direct bearing on how well public institutions serve citizens.

questions.question: Traditional rulers, labour unions, the press, religious bodies and student unions are all examples of:

options.a: Organs of the executive arm of government

questions.explanation: Each of these groups can affect or is affected by government decisions, so they are stakeholders in public governance, alongside citizens, NGOs, pressure groups, community leaders and civil servants. Option C refers to the legislature, executive and judiciary, Option A refers to ministries and agencies, and Option B refers to owners of company shares, none of which describes these groups.

questions.question: Residents of a community in Ogun State will live beside a new government landfill, bear its smell and health risks, and are demanding explanations from officials. In public governance terms, these residents are best described as:
questions.explanation: In public governance, stakeholders are those who gain from a public policy or bear its consequences and demand accountability, which fits the residents exactly. Option C enforces rules, Option D owns shares in companies, and Option B refers to government employees, none of which describes the community.

questions.question: Stakeholder theory was popularised by:
questions.explanation: R. Edward Freeman popularised stakeholder theory in 1984, arguing that organisations must manage the interests of everyone who affects or is affected by them. Option D is linked with work on authority and bureaucracy, Option C with the followership model, and Option B with social contract theory.

questions.question: In which year did R. Edward Freeman popularise stakeholder theory?
questions.explanation: Freeman popularised stakeholder theory in 1984. Option D is the year linked with Max Weber's work on authority and bureaucracy, Option B with Robert Kelley's followership model, and Option C with the stakeholder salience model of Mitchell, Agle and Wood.

questions.question: According to stakeholder theory, an organisation's long-term success depends on its ability to:

options.a: Concentrate every decision in the hands of top management
options.b: Identify, understand and manage the interests of multiple stakeholders
options.c: Avoid all contact with groups outside the organisation
options.d: Maximise returns to shareholders above all other interests

questions.explanation: Stakeholder theory holds that long-term success depends on identifying, understanding and managing the interests of the many groups that affect or are affected by the organisation. Option D is the shareholder-primacy view the theory rejects, and Options C and A shut stakeholders out instead of responding to them.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key governance implication of stakeholder theory?

options.a: Policy information is kept confidential from citizens
options.b: Decisions are made by leaders alone without consultation
options.c: Profit for shareholders becomes the only goal
