questions.question: Each of the four OGP eligibility areas carries a maximum of 4 points. What is the maximum total eligibility score for a country measured in all four areas?
questions.explanation: Four areas worth up to 4 points each give a maximum of 16, and a country needs at least 12 of them, which is 75 percent. Option B is the maximum for a single area. Option C is either the pass mark out of 16 or the maximum when one area is not measured, and Option D is not possible.

questions.question: When initiating a public sector reform, it helps to appoint a __________________ responsible for day-to-day coordination and reporting.
questions.explanation: Reform programmes usually set up a central reform secretariat or coordinating unit to manage day-to-day coordination, track progress and report to the leadership driving the reform. Option B is short-lived and political, while A and C would not give one clear point of continuous coordination.

questions.question: Regulatory reforms within the public sector focus on simplifying rules to reduce __________________
questions.explanation: Regulatory reform simplifies rules and procedures so that citizens and businesses spend less time and money complying, reducing administrative burden and compliance costs. Option A confuses regulatory reform with downsizing, while C and D are things reforms aim to strengthen, not reduce.

questions.question: Tracking reform performance using dashboards is an example of __________________
questions.explanation: Dashboards collect and display performance data for managers, which makes them a management information system tool for tracking reform progress. Options B, C and D are audit, oversight or risk exercises, not continuous data-tracking systems.

questions.question: Public sector reforms that institutionalize outcome reporting aim to present __________________
questions.explanation: Outcome reporting shows what was actually achieved compared with the targets that were set. Option C is tempting, but listing activities only describes effort and outputs, not results; B and D defeat the purpose of reporting.

questions.question: Successful reforms emphasise __________________ management to align staff performance with reform goals.
questions.explanation: Performance management sets targets, appraises staff and links their work to the goals of the reform. Option A (personnel management) handles general staffing matters such as hiring and records, while C and D deal with conflicts and emergencies.

questions.question: Strengthening asset management systems under public sector reforms improves __________________

options.d: Tracking and utilization of public assets

questions.explanation: Asset management systems record and monitor government property, which improves the tracking and proper utilisation of public assets. Options A, B and C describe the informal or political use of assets that such systems are designed to stop.

questions.question: The establishment of service delivery benchmarks under public sector reforms enables __________________
questions.explanation: Benchmarks set clear service standards, so the performance of agencies can be measured objectively against them. Option B is what benchmarks are meant to reduce, and A and C would make performance harder to judge fairly.

questions.question: Public sector reforms that integrate climate considerations aim to support __________________
questions.explanation: Building climate considerations into reforms helps the public sector plan for environmental risks, supporting sustainability and resilience. Option D is the opposite of long-term planning, and A and C have nothing to do with climate goals.

questions.question: The effectiveness of a public sector reform increases when its implementation timelines are:
questions.explanation: Realistic timelines match a reform's goals with the time, money and staff capacity actually available, so milestones can be met and progress tracked. Unrealistic deadlines (option B) lead to rushed or abandoned implementation, while undefined or arbitrary timelines (options C and D) make planning and monitoring impossible.

questions.question: The primary objective of public sector reform is to:

options.a: Reduce the size of government to eliminate all social programmes
options.b: Replace elected officials with technocratic managers
options.c: Improve the efficiency, effectiveness, accountability and responsiveness of government institutions and services
options.d: Transfer all public services to the private sector

questions.explanation: Public sector reforms are deliberate changes, such as restructuring, digitalisation and anti-corruption measures, meant to make government work better and deliver better services to citizens. Privatisation and downsizing can be tools of reform, but eliminating all social programmes (option A) or transferring every service (option D) are not the goal, and option B would undermine democracy.

questions.question: Which of the following is the FIRST critical step in initiating a public sector reform?

options.a: Comprehensive diagnosis and problem identification, including stakeholder consultations
options.b: Hiring international consultants to design the reform blueprint
options.c: Immediate restructuring of all government ministries
options.d: Passing new legislation without prior assessment

questions.explanation: A reform must start by understanding exactly what is wrong, why, and who is affected, because solutions designed without a clear diagnosis rarely fit local problems. Restructuring (option C) or new laws (option D) before assessment put action before understanding, and relying on outside consultants (option B) risks imported blueprints that do not fit the context.

questions.question: A feature of a successful public sector reform is:

options.a: Top-down imposition without consultation with affected stakeholders
options.b: Strong political will, clear leadership, broad stakeholder buy-in and sustained implementation commitment
options.c: Complete outsourcing of reform design to external consultants
options.d: Rapid implementation within a single budget cycle

questions.explanation: Reforms succeed when leaders are committed, the affected groups support the changes, and implementation is sustained long enough to change how institutions work. Lack of political will and resistance to change are common reasons reforms fail. Option A provokes resistance, option D is usually unrealistic, and option C weakens local ownership.

questions.question: New Public Management (NPM) as a reform approach advocates:

options.a: Eliminating all performance targets in the civil service
options.b: Expanding bureaucracy and centralising all decision-making
options.c: Restricting access to government services to reduce operational costs
options.d: Applying private sector management techniques to improve efficiency in public administration

questions.explanation: NPM brings business-style practices into government, such as results-based management, performance contracts, competition and contracting out services, to make public administration more efficient and results-focused. Option B is the rigid bureaucracy NPM reacts against, and options A and C contradict its emphasis on performance and service.

questions.question: Which of the following is a supporting condition necessary for public sector reforms to succeed?

options.a: Isolation from international best practices and peer learning
options.b: A politically neutral and capable civil service with reform capacity
options.c: Complete suppression of trade unions during reform implementation
options.d: Monopoly of the reform agenda by the presidency

questions.explanation: Reforms are carried out by public servants, so they need a professional, merit-based civil service with the skills and training to implement change. Option D removes broad ownership of the reform, option C breeds conflict and resistance, and option A cuts reformers off from useful lessons.

questions.question: An appropriate tool to measure the effectiveness of a public sector reform programme is:

options.a: The volume of legislation passed during the reform period
options.b: Independently verified performance indicators (KPIs), citizen satisfaction surveys and audit reports
options.c: Media sentiment analysis of government press releases
options.d: The personal judgment of the minister in charge

questions.explanation: Reform effectiveness should be measured objectively, using indicators such as revenue collected, service speed and quality, audited financial results and feedback from the citizens who use the services. A minister's opinion (option D) is not independent, and the number of laws passed (option A) or reactions to press releases (option C) measure activity or publicity rather than results.

questions.question: Nigeria's Integrated Payroll and Personnel Information System (IPPIS), introduced by the federal government in the mid-2000s, is an example of:

options.a: A public sector reform tool aimed at eliminating ghost workers and improving payroll transparency
options.b: A private sector HR management platform
options.c: A civil society initiative to improve education funding
options.d: An international debt management initiative by the World Bank

questions.explanation: IPPIS is a federal government digital payroll system that keeps personnel records and pays staff centrally, so that fictitious 'ghost workers' can be detected and removed and salary costs controlled. It is run by government, not civil society (option C) or a private company (option B), and although the World Bank helped fund its pilot, it is not a debt management scheme (option D).

questions.question: Which reform model focuses on building collaborative networks of public, private and civil society actors in service delivery?
questions.explanation: New Public Governance sees public services as delivered through partnerships and networks in which government works with businesses, NGOs and communities. The Weberian model (option A) and command-and-control governance (option D) rely on hierarchy within government, and Taylorism (option B) is about scientific work methods, not collaboration.

questions.question: Which approach to public sector reform focuses on solving specific local problems through step-by-step experimentation rather than copying 'best practice' blueprints?
questions.explanation: PDIA starts from a locally defined problem, tries out solutions, learns from the results and adapts, so reforms fit the real context instead of importing foreign templates. New Public Management (option D) applies private sector techniques, Weberian bureaucracy (option A) relies on fixed rules and hierarchy, and wholesale privatisation (option B) transfers services to private owners.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a successful public sector reform?

options.a: Retaining rigid, rule-bound procedures regardless of citizens' needs
options.d: A citizen-centred focus on improved service delivery

questions.explanation: Successful reforms aim to turn rigid, rule-based administrations into flexible institutions that deliver better value to citizens, so keeping rigid procedures regardless of need is the opposite of reform. Citizen-centred service delivery, digital transformation and professionalisation through merit and performance management (options D, B and C) are all features of successful reform.

questions.question: Nigeria's Treasury Single Account (TSA), which federal ministries, departments and agencies were directed to adopt in 2015, was mainly designed to:

options.a: Allow each agency to keep its revenue in multiple commercial bank accounts
options.b: Replace the Central Bank of Nigeria as the government's banker
options.c: Pay federal workers' salaries directly from World Bank funds
options.d: Consolidate government revenues into a single account to improve oversight and reduce leakages

questions.explanation: The TSA brings federal government revenues into a unified account structure so that the government can see and control all its cash, reducing hidden accounts, leakages and idle funds. Option A describes the fragmented system the TSA replaced, the TSA is operated with the Central Bank rather than replacing it (option B), and it has nothing to do with World Bank salary payments (option C).

questions.question: Nigeria's Government Integrated Financial Management Information System (GIFMIS) is mainly used as a reform tool to:

options.a: Issue national identity numbers to citizens
options.b: Regulate the prices of goods in public markets
options.d: Improve budgetary control and financial management across government

questions.explanation: GIFMIS is an IT-based public financial management system that records government spending against the budget and improves financial reporting, so its results can be used to judge whether financial management reforms are working. Voter registration (option C), national identity numbers (option A) and market price regulation (option B) are handled by other bodies and systems.

questions.question: Which of the following commonly limits the success of public sector reforms?

options.a: Strong citizen support for the reform
options.c: A clear and coherent reform strategy
options.d: Lack of political will and resistance to change

questions.explanation: Reforms often stall when leaders lack the commitment to see them through and when officials or interest groups who benefit from the old system resist change. Citizen support, continuous training and a clear strategy (options A, B and C) are conditions that help reforms succeed rather than obstacles.

questions.question: Deliberate, multifaceted initiatives designed to improve the efficiency, effectiveness, transparency and accountability of government machinery, in order to boost service delivery and institutional performance, are called ____.
questions.explanation: Public sector reforms are planned, many-sided changes to how government works, aimed at better service delivery and institutional performance. Option B concerns money supply and interest rates. Option C is a private-sector transaction, and Option D covers only one narrow area of reform.

questions.question: The success of public sector reforms depends heavily on ____.

options.a: the number of new ministries created
options.d: the age of the head of service

questions.explanation: Reforms often look good on paper, but their success depends on how well they are implemented and on sustained political will. Options A, C and D are not recognised determinants of reform success.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the major types of public sector reform initiative?
questions.explanation: Major reform types include civil service restructuring, e-governance, stronger financial management, anti-corruption measures and public-private partnerships. Reform aims to improve the civil service, not to abolish it. Options A, B and C are recognised types of reform.

questions.question: The introduction of 'due process' mechanisms in public procurement is a reform that mainly drives performance through ____.

options.d: centralising contract awards in one person

questions.explanation: Due process rules make procurement open and rule-based, which curbs corruption and improves accountability. Options A, B and D would weaken value for money and fairness rather than improve them.

questions.question: Re-professionalisation and training of public employees, which enhance professionalism and service delivery, are reform performance drivers classified under ____.
questions.explanation: Training and re-professionalising staff is capacity building, which raises the skills and professionalism of the workforce. Option A is about technology systems, and Option B transfers enterprises to private owners. Option D is a fiscal arrangement.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a common obstacle limiting the success of public sector reforms?
questions.explanation: Political instability, unclear strategies and resistance to change are common obstacles to reform. Strong political will is a condition for success, not an obstacle. Options B, C and D are the recognised challenges.

questions.question: Successful public sector reforms are characterised by a shift towards ____.
questions.explanation: Successful reforms move from rigid, rule-bound bureaucracy towards user-friendly, citizen-centred services, with more transparency and efficiency. Options B, C and D describe the traditional problems that reforms try to fix.

questions.question: A state government opens centres where citizens can register businesses, renew licences and obtain birth certificates under one roof instead of visiting several ministries. This BEST illustrates which feature of a successful reform?

options.d: Citizen-centric focus and improved service delivery (one-stop shops)

questions.explanation: One-stop shops, such as Kenya's Huduma Centres, put citizens' convenience at the centre of service delivery. Option A is about cutting excess staff and ghost workers, and Option B is an experimental, problem-solving method of reform. Option C transfers ownership to private investors.

questions.question: Huduma Centres, often cited as an example of citizen-centric one-stop shops for public services, are found in ____.
questions.explanation: Huduma Centres are Kenya's one-stop public service centres, used as an example of citizen-centric reform. Options A, B and C are other African countries that are not where these centres operate.

questions.question: Adopting private-sector practices in government, such as results-based management, performance contracting and contracting out services to create competition, is known as ____.
questions.explanation: New Public Management borrows private-sector tools such as results-based management, performance contracts and competition through contracting out. Option B is the rule-bound model that NPM tried to change. Options C and D are unrelated systems.

questions.question: A ministry signs agreements with its directors that set measurable targets for the year, and each director's continued appointment depends on meeting them. This NPM technique is called ____.
questions.explanation: Performance contracting ties managers to agreed, measurable targets and links their accountability to results. Option B reduces staff numbers or agencies, and Option C moves services onto digital platforms. Option D reveals who owns companies.

questions.question: Eliminating ghost workers, rationalising government agencies and streamlining processes to reduce costs is a reform feature known as ____.
questions.explanation: Right-sizing and restructuring cut waste, such as ghost workers and duplicated agencies, so that government runs at a sensible cost. Option A is about putting service users first, and Option B is about moving to digital platforms. Option D is a leadership concept.

questions.question: In public sector reform, a 'ghost worker' is ____.

options.a: an employee who works night shifts
options.b: a contract worker hired through an agency
options.c: a retired officer receiving a legitimate pension
options.d: a name on the government payroll that does not correspond to a real, working employee

questions.explanation: Ghost workers are fictitious or non-working names on the payroll whose salaries are stolen, and reforms such as IPPIS target them. Options A, B and C are all legitimate categories of workers or pensioners.

questions.question: Retraining staff, hiring on merit and using open performance appraisals are reform features grouped under ____.
questions.explanation: Professionalisation and performance management build a competent, merit-based workforce held accountable through open appraisal. Option A transfers ownership of enterprises, and Option B shifts authority to lower levels. Option D is an approach to solving local problems through experimentation.

questions.question: In public sector reform, PDIA stands for ____.
questions.explanation: PDIA stands for Problem-Driven Iterative Adaptation, a step-by-step reform approach. Options A, B and C are invented expansions that sound plausible but do not exist as this reform approach.

questions.question: Problem-Driven Iterative Adaptation (PDIA) is an approach to reform that ____.

options.a: copies successful reforms from other countries without change
options.b: solves specific local problems step by step through experimentation, rather than copying 'best practice' blueprints
options.c: implements all reforms at once in a single big-bang programme
options.d: leaves reform decisions entirely to foreign consultants

questions.explanation: PDIA starts from a concrete local problem and tries, learns and adapts in small steps, because imported blueprints may not fit the context. Option A is exactly what PDIA warns against. Option C is the opposite of iterative, and Option D ignores local ownership.

questions.question: Instead of adopting a foreign model wholesale, a state ministry of education tests three small changes in a few schools to reduce teacher absenteeism, keeps what works and adjusts the rest. This BEST illustrates ____.
questions.explanation: Testing small solutions to a specific local problem and adapting them based on results is the essence of PDIA. Option A hands services to outside providers. Option B is a cash-management reform, and Option D cuts staff or agencies.

questions.question: IPPIS, a key Nigerian public sector reform tool, stands for ____.

options.a: Integrated Payroll and Personnel Information System

questions.explanation: IPPIS is the Integrated Payroll and Personnel Information System, which centralises federal payroll and personnel records. Options B, C and D are invented names that sound similar but do not exist.

questions.question: The main purpose of Nigeria's IPPIS is to ____.

options.a: keep accurate personnel records and payroll, helping to detect and eliminate ghost workers
options.b: collect value added tax from companies

questions.explanation: IPPIS keeps payroll and personnel records accurate in one system, which exposes ghost workers and reduces payroll fraud. Option B is the work of the tax authority, Option C is the electoral commission's job, and Option D is the central bank's role.

questions.question: Nigeria's IPPIS project went live in April 2007 with a pilot covering how many federal MDAs?
questions.explanation: IPPIS went live in April 2007 with seven pilot MDAs and was then extended to more agencies over time. Options A and B are wrong figures. Option C ignores the phased roll-out.

questions.question: Since October 2008, IPPIS has been managed by which Nigerian federal office?

options.c: The Office of the Accountant-General of the Federation

questions.explanation: The Office of the Accountant-General of the Federation took over management of IPPIS in October 2008, which fits its role over federal payments. Options A, B and D are federal bodies with unrelated mandates.

questions.question: GIFMIS, a Nigerian public financial management reform, stands for ____.

options.a: General Internal Fund Monitoring and Inspection Scheme
options.b: Government Integrated Financial Management Information System
options.c: Government Investment Fund for Micro Industries Scheme
options.d: Global Integrated Finance and Monetary Index System

questions.explanation: GIFMIS is the Government Integrated Financial Management Information System, used to improve budgetary control and financial reporting. Options A, C and D are invented expansions.

questions.question: Which pairing of Nigerian reform tool and its main contribution is CORRECT?

options.a: IPPIS - improving budgetary control; GIFMIS - reducing ghost workers
options.b: IPPIS - reducing payroll fraud (ghost workers); GIFMIS - improving budgetary control
options.c: IPPIS - conducting elections; GIFMIS - issuing passports
options.d: IPPIS - collecting customs duty; GIFMIS - regulating telecoms

questions.explanation: IPPIS cleans up payroll and personnel records, cutting ghost workers, while GIFMIS strengthens budgeting and financial management. Option A swaps the two tools. Options C and D assign functions belonging to unrelated agencies.

questions.question: The Treasury Single Account (TSA) is a reform that ____.

options.a: allows each ministry to open as many commercial bank accounts as it wishes
options.b: transfers all government money to foreign banks
options.d: consolidates government revenues into a unified account to centralise revenue, improve oversight and reduce leakages

questions.explanation: TSA brings government agencies' inflows together in a unified account structure at the Central Bank of Nigeria, which improves oversight and reduces leakages. Option A describes the fragmented system that TSA replaced. Options B and C are not what TSA does.

questions.question: Nigeria's Treasury Single Account consolidates federal government agencies' inflows into an account held at ____.
questions.explanation: The TSA is held at the Central Bank of Nigeria, which acts as the government's banker. Option A is an international lender, and Option C is a securities market. Option D collects taxes but does not hold the TSA.

questions.question: Nigeria's TSA was piloted in 2012. Under which administration was full implementation across all federal MDAs mandated in 2015?
questions.explanation: TSA was initiated under President Jonathan, with a pilot in 2012, and the Buhari administration mandated full implementation across all federal MDAs in 2015. Options A and B led Nigeria before TSA was introduced. Option D took office in 2023, long after full implementation.

questions.question: Reforms such as the Treasury Single Account have been credited with which effect on Nigerian government finances?

options.b: Eliminating the need for a national budget
options.c: Increasing the number of ghost workers

questions.explanation: TSA and related reforms have been credited with raising Internally Generated Revenue and reducing ghost workers, although their overall impact is still mixed. Options B and D overstate any reform's effect. Option C is the opposite of what these reforms achieve.

questions.question: Establishing anti-corruption bodies such as the EFCC and ICPC is classified as which kind of core public sector reform component?
questions.explanation: Restructuring agencies, privatising public enterprises and creating anti-corruption bodies such as the EFCC and ICPC are structural and institutional reforms. Option A covers systems such as IPPIS and GIFMIS, and Option C covers capacity, ethics and performance management. Option D is the central bank's domain.

questions.question: Strengthening capacity, enforcing ethics and implementing performance management systems are grouped under which core component of public sector reform?
questions.explanation: Capacity, ethics and performance management concern people and administration, so they are administrative and human resource reforms. Option A covers regulators and procurement rules. Option B covers tools such as TSA, and Option D covers electronic systems.

questions.question: The law that established Nigeria's Bureau of Public Procurement and put the 'due process' approach to public procurement on a statutory footing is the ____.
questions.explanation: The Public Procurement Act 2007 created the Bureau of Public Procurement and gave legal backing to due process in procurement. Option A deals with access to information, and Option B regulates companies. Option C deals with fiscal discipline and budgeting, not procurement procedures.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the key objectives of public sector reforms?
questions.explanation: Reforms aim to enhance service delivery, combat corruption, modernise the economy by reducing the cost of governance, and strengthen institutions. Increasing the cost of governance is the opposite of economic modernisation. Options A, C and D are listed objectives.

questions.question: The public sector reform objective of 'economic modernisation' involves ____.

options.a: increasing the number of government agencies
options.c: aligning public services with market demands and reducing the cost of governance

questions.explanation: Economic modernisation means aligning public services with the needs of the market and cutting the cost of running government. Option A usually raises costs, Option B contradicts reforms such as PPPs, and Option D reverses digitalisation.

questions.question: Nigeria's Bureau of Public Service Reforms (BPSR) was established by the Federal Government in ____.
questions.explanation: The BPSR was established by the Federal Government on 4 February 2004 to drive public service reforms. Option A is the year of the return to civil rule. Option C is the year of the Freedom of Information Act, and Option D is the year Nigeria joined OGP.

questions.question: The mandate of Nigeria's Bureau of Public Service Reforms (BPSR) is BEST described as ____.

options.a: to prosecute corrupt public officials in court
options.b: to initiate, coordinate, monitor and ensure full implementation of government reform policies and programmes
options.c: to print and issue the national currency
options.d: to conduct recruitment examinations for universities

questions.explanation: The BPSR exists to initiate, coordinate, monitor and ensure full implementation of government reform policies and programmes. Option A is the role of anti-graft agencies and the courts. Option C belongs to the central bank, and Option D to examination bodies.

questions.question: When initiating a public sector reform, why should baseline data on current performance be collected before changes begin?

options.a: So that later results can be compared with the starting position to show whether the reform worked
options.b: So that the reform can avoid having any targets
options.c: Because baseline data replaces the need for implementation
options.d: So that stakeholders do not need to be consulted

questions.explanation: Baseline data records performance before the reform, which makes it possible to measure improvement afterwards. Option B is wrong because baselines are used to set targets. Options C and D misunderstand what a baseline is for.

questions.question: Why do reformers often pilot a reform in a few agencies before rolling it out nationwide, as Nigeria did when IPPIS started with seven MDAs?

options.a: To make sure most agencies never adopt the reform
options.b: To avoid measuring the reform's results
options.c: To test the reform, learn from problems and fix them before scaling up
options.d: Because piloting removes all resistance to change

questions.explanation: Piloting lets reformers test the design on a small scale, learn lessons and adjust it before national roll-out, which lowers risk. Option A defeats the purpose of reform, and Option B is wrong because pilots are evaluated. Option D overstates what piloting can do.

questions.question: A state government plans to merge two overlapping agencies. Staff fear job losses and rumours are spreading. Which step in initiating the reform would MOST directly address this resistance?

options.a: Announcing the merger only after it is complete
options.b: Communicating the reasons for the change clearly and engaging staff and unions early

questions.explanation: Resistance to change is reduced when people understand why a reform is needed and are consulted early, so a clear communication and engagement plan is a key step when initiating reform. Options A and C would deepen distrust. Option D would undermine the reform's purpose.

questions.question: When initiating a public sector reform, identifying a reform 'champion' at senior political level is important MAINLY because ____.

options.a: it removes the need for any civil servants
options.b: it guarantees the reform will cost nothing
options.c: it provides the political will and leadership needed to drive the reform and overcome resistance
options.d: it ensures the reform will not be evaluated

questions.explanation: A senior champion supplies the sustained political will that reforms depend on and helps to overcome resistance. Option A is unrealistic, and Option B is false. Option D is wrong because a good champion wants results to be measured.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a supporting condition for a successful public sector reform?

options.b: Frequent changes of reform leadership and strategy

questions.explanation: Reforms need sustained political will, adequate resources, capable staff, a clear strategy and stakeholder support. Frequent changes in leadership and strategy cause the political instability and lack of clear strategy that block reforms. Options A, C and D are genuine supporting conditions.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key challenge that limits the effectiveness of public sector reforms in Nigeria?

options.a: Implementation gaps arising from lack of political will and poor strategic planning

questions.explanation: Implementation gaps caused by weak political will and poor planning, together with resource constraints and capacity needs, limit reform effectiveness. Options B, C and D describe conditions that would help reforms rather than hinder them.

questions.question: Measuring the effectiveness of public sector reforms in Nigeria involves assessing improvements mainly in ____.

options.a: transparency, financial accountability and service delivery
options.b: the popularity of the ruling party
options.c: the number of new government buildings
options.d: the salaries of political office holders

questions.explanation: Reform effectiveness is judged by gains in transparency, financial accountability and service delivery, often tracked through systems such as IPPIS and GIFMIS. Options B, C and D are not valid measures of whether reforms are working.

questions.question: Assessing the speed, quality and accessibility of public services, and the impact of due process in procurement, is which category of indicator for measuring reform effectiveness?
questions.explanation: Speed, quality and accessibility of services, plus the effects of due process, are service delivery and efficiency indicators. Option A looks at growth and wider development indicators. Option C looks at anti-graft agencies and IPSAS, and Option D looks at revenue, payroll fraud and budget control.

questions.question: Evaluating how effective anti-graft agencies (EFCC, ICPC) are, and how well International Public Sector Accounting Standards (IPSAS) have been implemented, falls under which category of reform effectiveness indicator?
questions.explanation: The effectiveness of anti-corruption bodies and the adoption of IPSAS measure how much stronger institutions have become. Option B measures the speed and quality of services, and Option C measures broader growth. Option D is a feature of successful reform, not an indicator category.

questions.question: In public sector reform, IPSAS stands for ____.

options.c: International Procurement and Supply Audit Standards

questions.explanation: IPSAS are the International Public Sector Accounting Standards, used to improve the quality and comparability of government financial reports. Options A, B and C are invented expansions.

questions.question: A tool in which citizens rate the availability, quality and responsiveness of public services through surveys, giving agencies direct user feedback on reform results, is called a ____.
questions.explanation: Citizen report cards and satisfaction surveys measure reform effectiveness from the service user's point of view. Option A is a cash-management reform, and Option C checks payroll records. Option D is a request to join an initiative such as OGP.

questions.question: Comparing an agency's performance indicators with those of similar agencies, or with recognised good-practice standards, in order to judge reform progress is called ____.
questions.explanation: Benchmarking measures performance against peers or standards to show where an agency stands and how far it has improved. Option A is a crisis-response strategy of blaming others. Option B is a restructuring feature, and Option D is joint design of plans with civil society.

questions.question: An independent examination, often carried out by the Auditor-General, of whether a public programme achieved economy, efficiency and effectiveness, is called a ____.
questions.explanation: A performance or value-for-money audit tests whether a programme delivered the three Es, not just whether its accounts balance. Option A checks the accuracy of financial reports only. Option B counts the population, and Option C is a crisis communication tool.

questions.question: To evaluate a payroll reform, a ministry compares the number of names on its payroll and its monthly wage bill before and after the reform, and finds 1,200 fictitious names removed. The ministry is measuring reform effectiveness mainly through ____.
questions.explanation: Reduced payroll fraud and a lower wage bill are financial performance and accountability indicators, the kind IPPIS is meant to improve. Option B would look at growth and wider development, and Option C would ask service users for their views. Option D is unrelated to payroll.

questions.question: A survey that follows public funds from the central government through each level down to frontline units such as schools and clinics, to find out how much actually arrives, is called a ____.
questions.explanation: A Public Expenditure Tracking Survey traces the flow of money to frontline service units and shows leakages along the way, which makes it a useful tool for measuring financial management reforms. Option A collects users' views of service quality rather than tracing funds. Options B and C measure population and company ownership.

questions.question: Which list correctly states the key objectives of public sector reform?

options.a: Decentralisation, PDIA, New Public Management techniques and digital transformation
options.b: Political instability, lack of strategy and resistance to change
options.c: Enhancing service delivery, combating corruption, economic modernisation and strengthening institutions
options.d: Civil service restructuring, IFMIS and public-private partnerships

questions.explanation: The key objectives of public sector reform are to enhance service delivery, combat corruption, achieve economic modernisation and strengthen institutions. Option B lists common obstacles to reform, Option A lists features of successful reforms, and Option D lists major reform initiatives rather than the objectives they serve.

questions.question: A state government introduces a reform whose main aim is to stop officials from inflating contract prices and diverting public funds into private pockets. Which objective of public sector reform is it chiefly pursuing?
questions.explanation: Stopping contract inflation and the diversion of public funds is directly about combating corruption. Option C focuses on how well citizens are served, Option D on modernising the economy and the cost of governance, and Option B on building the capacity of public bodies, none of which is the main aim described.

questions.question: A federal reform cuts the time citizens wait to receive their international passports from six weeks to one week. Which objective of public sector reform does this mainly serve?
questions.explanation: Making a public service faster and easier for citizens to obtain is enhancing service delivery. Option D is about stopping abuse of office, Option A is about modernising the economy and reducing the cost of governance, and Option C is about building the capacity and independence of public bodies.
